en: Thus have I heard: the Satipaṭṭhāna Sutta, the tenth discourse of the Majjhima Nikāya.
On one occasion the Blessed One was dwelling among the Kurus at a Kuru town named Kammāsadhamma.
There the Blessed One addressed the bhikkhus: "Bhikkhus!"
“Venerable Sir,” those monks replied to the Blessed One.
The Blessed One said this:

“Monks, this is the one-way path for the purification of beings, for the surmounting of sorrow and lamentation, for the disappearance of pain and grief, for the attainment of the true way, and for the realization of nibbāna.”
For the cessation of suffering and mental distress, for the attainment of the true method, and for the realization of Nibbāna— namely,
the four foundations of mindfulness.
What are the four?
Here, monks, a bhikkhu dwells contemplating the body in the body, ardent, clearly comprehending, and mindful, having removed covetousness and displeasure regarding the world;
he dwells contemplating feelings in feelings, ardent, clearly comprehending, and mindful, having removed covetousness and displeasure regarding the world;
he dwells contemplating the mind in the mind, ardent, clearly comprehending, and mindful, having removed covetousness and displeasure regarding the world.
He dwells contemplating phenomena in phenomena, ardent, clearly comprehending, and mindful, having removed covetousness and displeasure regarding the world.
The summary is finished.
1. Contemplation of the Body.
1.1. The Section on Mindfulness of Breathing in the Contemplation of the Body And how, monks, does a monk dwell contemplating the body as the body?
Here, monks, a monk, having gone to the forest, or to the foot of a tree, or to an empty hut, sits down; folding his legs crosswise, setting his body erect, and establishing mindfulness before him.
Thus, he breathes in mindfully and breathes out mindfully.
Breathing in long, he understands: "I am breathing in long"; breathing out long, he understands: "I am breathing out long.
Breathing in short, he understands: "I am breathing in short"; breathing out short, he understands: "I am breathing out short."
‘Experiencing the whole body, I shall breathe in,’ he trains himself; ‘experiencing the whole body, I shall breathe out,’ he trains himself.
‘Tranquillizing the bodily formation, I shall breathe in,’ he trains himself; ‘tranquillizing the bodily formation, I shall breathe out,’ he trains himself.
Just as, monks, a skilled turner or a turner’s apprentice, when turning a long turn, understands, ‘I am making a long turn,’ or when turning a short turn, understands, ‘I am making a short turn’;
In the same way, monks, when a monk breathes in long, he understands:
"I am breathing in long"; when he breathes out long, he understands: "I am breathing out long. When he breathes in short, he understands:
"I am breathing in short"; when he breathes out short, he understands: "I am breathing out short."
He trains thus: "I shall breathe in experiencing the whole body"; he trains thus: "I shall breathe out experiencing the whole body.
He trains thus: "I shall breathe in tranquilizing the bodily formation"; he trains thus: "I shall breathe out tranquilizing the bodily formation.

Thus, he dwells contemplating the body in the body internally, or he dwells contemplating the body in the body externally, or he dwells contemplating the body in the body both internally and externally.

Or he dwells contemplating the nature of origination in the body; or he dwells contemplating the nature of vanishing in the body; or he dwells contemplating the nature of both origination and vanishing in the body.
Or else, mindfulness that "there is a body" is established in him to the extent necessary for bare knowledge and for mindfulness. And he dwells independent, not clinging to anything in the world.
It is in this way, monks, that a monk dwells contemplating the body in the body.
The Section on Mindfulness of Breathing is finished. 1.2.

The Section on Postures in the Contemplation of the Body Furthermore, monks, when walking, a monk understands: "I am walking"; when standing, he understands: "I am standing"; when sitting, he understands: "I am sitting"; and when lying down, he understands: "I am lying down."
Or, in whatever way his body is disposed, he understands it accordingly.

Thus, he dwells contemplating the body in the body internally, or he dwells contemplating the body in the body externally, or he dwells contemplating the body in the body both internally and externally;

or he dwells contemplating the nature of origination in the body, or he dwells contemplating the nature of dissolution in the body, or he dwells contemplating the nature of both origination and dissolution in the body.

Or else, mindfulness that “there is a body” is established in him to the extent necessary for bare knowledge and for constant mindfulness. And he abides independent, not clinging to anything in the world.
It is in this way, monks, that a monk dwells contemplating the body as a body.
The section on postures is finished.
1.3. The Section on Full Awareness in the Contemplation of the Body Furthermore, monks, a monk acts with full awareness when going forward and returning;

he acts with full awareness when looking ahead and looking aside; he acts with full awareness when bending and stretching his limbs; he acts with full awareness in carrying his outer robe, bowl, and inner robes.
He acts with clear comprehension when eating, drinking, chewing, and tasting; he acts with clear comprehension in discharging excrement and urine;
he acts with clear comprehension in walking, standing, sitting, sleeping, waking, speaking, and remaining silent.
Thus, he dwells contemplating the body in the body internally... [and so on].
In this way too, monks, a monk dwells contemplating the body in the body.
The section on clear comprehension is finished. 1.4.
The Section on Contemplation of the Body through Attention to Repulsiveness.
Furthermore, monks, a monk reviews this very body, from the soles of the feet upwards and from the hair of the head downwards, bounded by the skin, as full of various kinds of impurity:
"In this body there are head-hairs, body-hairs, nails, teeth, skin, flesh, sinews,
bones, bone-marrow, kidneys, heart, liver, midriff, spleen, lungs, intestines, mesentery, gorge, feces, bile..."
"Phlegm, pus, blood, sweat, fat, tears, grease, spittle, snot, synovial fluid, and urine.

Monks, it is just as if there were a two-mouthed bag full of various kinds of grain, such as rice, barley, mung beans, black gram, sesame seeds, and husked rice. A man with good eyesight, having opened it, would examine it:
‘This is rice, this is barley, these are mung beans, these are black grams, these are sesame seeds, these are husked rice.
In the same way, monks, a monk contemplates this very body—up from the soles of the feet and down from the hair of the head, bounded by the skin, full of various kinds of impurity:
‘In this body there are head hairs, body hairs... [and so on] ... urine.’
"Thus, monks, a monk dwells contemplating the body as a body internally...
In this way too, monks, a monk dwells contemplating the body as a body.
The section on the contemplation of repulsiveness is finished."
1.5. The Section on Attention to the Elements in the Mindfulness of the Body Furthermore, monks, a monk reviews this very body, however it is placed or disposed, in terms of its elements:
"In this body there are the earth element, the water element, the fire element, and the air element."
“Just as if, monks, a skilled butcher or a butcher’s apprentice, having slaughtered a cow, were sitting at a crossroads after dividing it into portions;
even so, monks, a monk reviews this very body, however it is placed or disposed, according to its elements:
‘In this body there is the earth element, the water element, the fire element, and the air element.’”
"Thus, monks, a monk dwells contemplating the body in the body internally...
In this way too, monks, a monk dwells contemplating the body in the body.
The section on attention to elements is finished."

1.6. The Section on the Nine Cemetery Contemplations in Mindfulness of the Body Furthermore, monks, suppose a monk were to see a body discarded in a charnel ground, dead for one day, or dead for two days, or dead for three days—swollen, discolored, and festering. He compares this very body with it: "This body, too, is of the same nature; it will not escape this condition. This, monks, is a higher perception that is noble, supramundane, and a factor of enlightenment. Furthermore, monks, suppose a monk were to see a body discarded in a charnel ground, dead for four or five days, or seven days, being devoured by crows, hawks, vultures, dogs, jackals, or various kinds of worms. He compares this very body with it: "This body, too, is of the same nature; it will not escape this condition. This, monks, is a higher perception that is noble, supramundane, and a factor of enlightenment. Furthermore, monks, suppose a monk were to see a body discarded in a charnel ground, reduced to a skeleton with some flesh and blood adhering to it, held together by sinews... [or] a skeleton without flesh, smeared with blood, held together by sinews... [or] a skeleton without flesh and blood, held together by sinews... [or] disconnected bones scattered in all directions—here a hand-bone, there a foot-bone, here a shin-bone, there a thigh-bone, here a hip-bone, there a backbone, and there the skull. He compares this very body with it: "This body, too, is of the same nature; it will not escape this condition. This, monks, is a higher perception that is noble, supramundane, and a factor of enlightenment. Furthermore, monks, suppose a monk were to see a body discarded in a charnel ground, reduced to bones, more than a year old, bleached to the color of shells... [or] a heap of bones gathered together... [or] bones decayed and crumbled to dust. He compares this very body with it: "This body, too, is of the same nature; it will not escape this condition. This, monks, is a higher perception that is noble, supramundane, and a factor of enlightenment.
‘This body, too, is of such a nature, of such a character, and not exempt from this.
Thus, monks, a monk dwells contemplating the body in the body internally...
In this way, monks, a monk dwells contemplating the body in the body.
Furthermore, monks, suppose a monk were to see a body discarded in a charnel ground,
being devoured by crows, or being devoured by hawks, or being devoured by vultures,
or being devoured by herons, or being devoured by dogs, or being devoured by tigers, or being devoured by leopards.
Or being devoured by jackals, or being devoured by various kinds of worms.
He applies this to his own body:
"This body, too, is of such a nature, of such a character, and not exempt from this."
Thus, monks, a monk dwells contemplating the body as a body internally … [as before] … In this way too, monks, a monk dwells contemplating the body as a body. Furthermore, monks,

suppose a monk were to see a corpse discarded in a charnel ground— a skeleton with flesh and blood still adhering, bound together by sinews … [as before] … In this way too, monks, a monk dwells contemplating the body as a body.
A skeleton, smeared with flesh and blood, bound together by sinews; ...
a skeleton, devoid of flesh and blood, bound together by sinews; ...
bones detached from their connections, scattered in all directions—here a hand-bone, there a [foot]-bone...
The foot bone by one side, the ankle bone by another, the shin bone by another, the thigh bone by another, the hip bone by another,
the spine bone by another, the shoulder blade bone by another,
the neck bone by another, the jaw bone by another, the tooth bone by another, and the skull by another.
He applies this very body [as a comparison]:
"This body, too, is of such a nature, of such a character, and not exempt from this condition.
Thus, he dwells contemplating the body as a body internally... [and so on].
In this way too, monks, a monk dwells contemplating the body in the body.
Furthermore, monks, suppose a monk were to see a corpse discarded in a charnel ground—bones whitened, resembling the color of a conch shell...
[and so on] ...bones heaped up, more than three years old... [and so on].
Bones that are putrid and reduced to powder.
He applies this to his own body:
"This body, too, is of such a nature, of such a character, and not exempt from this fate."

Thus he dwells contemplating the body in the body internally, or he dwells contemplating the body in the body externally, or he dwells contemplating the body in the body both internally and externally.

Or else he dwells contemplating in the body its nature of arising, or he dwells contemplating in the body its nature of passing away, or he dwells contemplating in the body its nature of both arising and passing away.
Or else mindfulness that "there is a body" is established in him to the extent necessary for bare knowledge and for mindfulness. And he dwells independent, not clinging to anything in the world.
In this way too, monks, a monk dwells contemplating the body as a body.
The section on the nine charnel-ground contemplations is finished.
The fourteen contemplations of the body are finished.
2. Contemplation of Feelings.
And how, monks, does a monk dwell contemplating feelings in feelings?
Here, monks, when feeling a pleasant feeling, a monk understands: "I am feeling a pleasant feeling."
When experiencing a painful feeling, one understands: "I am experiencing a painful feeling.
When experiencing a neither-painful-nor-pleasant feeling, one understands: "I am experiencing a neither-painful-nor-pleasant feeling.
When experiencing a sensual pleasant feeling, one understands: "I am experiencing a sensual pleasant feeling."
When experiencing a spiritual pleasant feeling, one understands: "I am experiencing a spiritual pleasant feeling.
When experiencing a worldly painful feeling, one understands: "I am experiencing a worldly painful feeling.
When experiencing a spiritual painful feeling, one understands: "I am experiencing a spiritual painful feeling."
When feeling a worldly neither-painful-nor-pleasant feeling, one understands: "I feel a worldly neither-painful-nor-pleasant feeling.
When feeling an unworldly neither-painful-nor-pleasant feeling, one understands: "I feel an unworldly neither-painful-nor-pleasant feeling.

Thus, one dwells contemplating feelings in feelings internally, or one dwells contemplating feelings in feelings externally, or one dwells contemplating feelings in feelings both internally and externally.

Or he dwells contemplating the nature of arising in feelings, or he dwells contemplating the nature of vanishing in feelings, or he dwells contemplating the nature of both arising and vanishing in feelings.
Or else, mindfulness that "there is feeling" is established in him to the extent necessary for bare knowledge and mindfulness; and he dwells independent, not clinging to anything in the world.
It is in this way, monks, that a monk dwells contemplating feelings in feelings.
The contemplation of feelings is finished.
3. Contemplation of the Mind:
And how, monks, does a monk dwell contemplating the mind in the mind?
In this case, monks, a monk understands a mind affected by lust as ‘a mind affected by lust.
He understands a mind free from lust as ‘a mind free from lust.
He understands a mind affected by hatred as ‘a mind affected by hatred.’
He understands a mind free from hatred as "a mind free from hatred.
He understands a deluded mind as "a deluded mind.
He understands a mind free from delusion as "a mind free from delusion."
He understands a contracted mind as ‘a contracted mind.
He understands a scattered mind as ‘a scattered mind.
He understands a magnified mind as ‘a magnified mind.’
He understands an unexalted mind as "an unexalted mind.
He understands a surpassable mind as "a surpassable mind.
He understands an unsurpassable mind as "an unsurpassable mind."
He understands a concentrated mind as “a concentrated mind”;
he understands an unconcentrated mind as “an unconcentrated mind”;
he understands a liberated mind as “a liberated mind.”
Or, when the mind is unliberated, he understands, "The mind is unliberated.

Thus, he dwells contemplating the mind in the mind internally, or he dwells contemplating the mind in the mind externally, or he dwells contemplating the mind in the mind both internally and externally;

or he dwells contemplating the nature of arising in the mind, or he dwells contemplating the nature of passing away in the mind, or he dwells contemplating the nature of both arising and passing away in the mind.
Or else, mindfulness that ‘there is mind’ is established in him. To this extent he abides independent, mindful and clearly comprehending, and does not cling to anything in the world.
In this way too, monks, a monk dwells contemplating the mind in the mind.
Contemplation of the mind is finished.
4. Contemplation of Mental Objects (Dhammānupassanā) 4.1.
The Section on the Hindrances (Nīvaraṇapabba) And how, monks, does a monk dwell contemplating mental objects as mental objects?
“Here, monks, a monk dwells contemplating phenomena among phenomena with regard to the five hindrances.
And how, monks, does a monk dwell contemplating phenomena among phenomena with regard to the five hindrances?
Here, monks, if sensual desire is present within him, a monk knows: ‘Sensual desire is present within me.’”
He understands it; or, when sensual desire is absent within him, he understands:

"There is no sensual desire in me. He understands how the arising of unarisen sensual desire comes about, and he understands how the abandoning of arisen sensual desire comes about, and he understands how, once abandoned, sensual desire will not arise again in the future.
There is non-arising, and he understands that.
Or, when ill will is present within him, he understands: "There is ill will within me";
or when ill will is not present within him, he understands: "There is no ill will within me. And he understands how unarisen [ill will]...
There is the arising of ill will, and he understands that; he understands how there comes to be the abandoning of arisen ill will;
and he understands how there comes to be the non-arising of abandoned ill will in the future.
Or, when sloth and torpor are present within him, he understands: "There is sloth and torpor in me"; when they are absent...
Or, when there is no sloth and torpor within him, he understands: "There is no sloth and torpor within me.
He understands how the arising of unarisen sloth and torpor comes about; he understands how the abandoning of arisen sloth and torpor comes about;
and he understands how the non-arising of abandoned sloth and torpor will come about in the future.
When restlessness and remorse are present within him, he understands: "There is restlessness and remorse within me";
or when restlessness and remorse are not present within him, he understands: "There is no restlessness and remorse within me.
And he understands how there comes to be the arising of unarisen restlessness and remorse, and how...
He understands the abandoning of arisen restlessness and remorse;
he understands how there is no further arising of abandoned restlessness and remorse in the future.
Or, when doubt is present within him, he understands: "There is doubt within me"; when it is absent...
Or, when there is doubt internally, he understands, ‘There is no doubt within me.
He understands how the arising of unarisen doubt comes about, and he understands how the abandoning of arisen doubt comes about,
and he understands how the non-arising of abandoned doubt will come about in the future.

Thus he dwells contemplating phenomena in phenomena internally, or he dwells contemplating phenomena in phenomena externally, or he dwells contemplating phenomena in phenomena both internally and externally;

or he dwells contemplating the nature of arising in phenomena, or he dwells contemplating the nature of passing away in phenomena, or he dwells contemplating the nature of both arising and passing away in phenomena.

Or else, mindfulness that ‘there are mental phenomena’ is established in him. To this extent he remains independent, not clinging to anything in the world, possessing mere knowledge and mere mindfulness.
It is in this way, monks, that a monk dwells contemplating mental phenomena as mental phenomena in regard to the five hindrances.
The section on the hindrances is finished.
4.2. The Section on the Aggregates in the Contemplation of Phenomena Furthermore, monks, a monk dwells contemplating phenomena among phenomena in regard to the five aggregates of clinging.
And how, monks, does a monk dwell contemplating phenomena among phenomena in regard to the five aggregates of clinging?
In this case, monks, a bhikkhu [understands]:
"Such is form, such its origin, such its passing away;
such is feeling, such its origin, such its passing away."
‘Such is perception, such is the origin of perception, such is the passing away of perception;
such are volitional formations, such is the origin of volitional formations, such is the passing away of volitional formations;
such is consciousness, such is the origin of consciousness, such is the passing away of consciousness.’”

Thus he dwells contemplating phenomena in phenomena internally, or he dwells contemplating phenomena in phenomena externally, or he dwells contemplating phenomena in phenomena both internally and externally;

or he dwells contemplating the nature of arising in phenomena, or he dwells contemplating the nature of passing away in phenomena, or he dwells contemplating the nature of both arising and passing away in phenomena.
Or else, mindfulness that ‘there are phenomena’ is established in him. This is merely for the sake of knowledge and mindfulness; he dwells independent and does not cling to anything in the world.
In this way, monks, a monk dwells contemplating phenomena as phenomena in regard to the five aggregates of clinging.
The section on the aggregates is finished.

4.3. The Section on the Bases (Āyatana) in the Contemplation of Phenomena (Dhammānupassanā) Furthermore, monks, a monk dwells contemplating phenomena as phenomena in regard to the six internal and external bases.
And how, monks, does a monk dwell contemplating phenomena as phenomena in regard to the six internal and external bases?
Here, monks, a bhikkhu understands the eye, he understands forms, and he understands the fetter that arises dependent upon both;
he understands how there comes to be the arising of an unarisen fetter, and he understands how there comes to be the abandoning of a fetter once arisen. And how...
And he understands the non-arising in the future of that fetter which has been abandoned.

He understands the ear; he understands sounds; and he understands the fetter that arises dependent upon both of these, as well as how the arising of a fetter that has not yet arisen occurs—and that he understands. How...
He understands the abandoning of the arisen fetter, and he understands how there is the non-arising of the abandoned fetter in the future.
He understands the nose, he understands odors, and he understands the fetter that arises dependent upon both.
And he understands that; he understands how there is the arising of an unarisen fetter;
he understands how there is the abandoning of an arisen fetter; and he understands how there is the future non-arising of an abandoned fetter.
He understands the tongue; he understands tastes; he understands the fetter that arises dependent upon both;
he understands how there comes to be the arising of an unarisen fetter; he understands how there comes to be the abandoning of an arisen fetter;
and he understands how there comes to be the non-arising of a fetter once it has been abandoned.
He understands its non-arising in the future.
He understands the body; he understands tangible objects; he understands the fetter that arises dependent upon both;
and he understands how the arising of an unarisen fetter occurs. And how...
He understands the abandoning of the arisen fetter, and he understands how there comes to be the non-arising of the abandoned fetter in the future.
He understands the mind, he understands mental phenomena, and he understands the fetter that arises dependent upon both.
And he understands that; he understands how there is the arising of an unarisen fetter;
he understands how there is the abandoning of a fetter that has arisen; and he understands how there is the non-arising in the future of a fetter that has been abandoned.

Thus he dwells contemplating phenomena in phenomena internally, or he dwells contemplating phenomena in phenomena externally, or he dwells contemplating phenomena in phenomena both internally and externally;

or he dwells contemplating in phenomena the phenomenon of arising, or he dwells contemplating in phenomena the phenomenon of passing away, or he dwells contemplating in phenomena the phenomenon of both arising and passing away.
Or else, mindfulness that “there are phenomena” is established in him, just for the sake of bare knowledge and bare mindfulness; and he dwells independent, not clinging to anything in the world.
In this way too, monks, a monk dwells contemplating phenomena as phenomena in regard to the six internal and external sense bases.
The section on the sense bases is finished.

4.4. The Section on the Factors of Enlightenment in the Contemplation of Phenomena Furthermore, monks, a monk dwells contemplating phenomena among phenomena in regard to the seven factors of enlightenment.
And how, monks, does a monk dwell contemplating phenomena among phenomena in regard to the seven factors of enlightenment?
In this case, monks, a monk, when the enlightenment factor of mindfulness is present within him, understands: ‘The enlightenment factor of mindfulness is present within me’;
or when the enlightenment factor of mindfulness is not present within him, he understands: ‘The enlightenment factor of mindfulness is not present within me’;
and he understands how the unarisen enlightenment factor of mindfulness comes to arise.

And he understands how there comes to be the fulfillment of the development of the mindfulness enlightenment factor that has arisen; and he understands how there comes to be the fulfillment of the development of the investigation-of-phenomena enlightenment factor that has arisen.
Or, when the investigation-of-phenomena enlightenment factor is present within him, he understands: "The investigation-of-phenomena enlightenment factor is present within me";
or when the investigation-of-phenomena enlightenment factor is not present within him, he understands: "The investigation-of-phenomena enlightenment factor is not present within me."
He understands it; he understands how there comes to be the arising of the unarisen investigation-of-dharmas enlightenment factor;
and he understands how there comes to be the fulfillment by development of the arisen investigation-of-dharmas enlightenment factor.
Or, when the energy enlightenment factor is present within him, he understands: "The energy enlightenment factor is present within me."
He understands it; or, if the enlightenment factor of energy is absent within him, he understands: "The enlightenment factor of energy is not present within me.

He understands how there comes to be the arising of the unarisen enlightenment factor of energy, and he understands how there comes to be the fulfillment by development of the enlightenment factor of energy once it has arisen.
When the enlightenment factor of rapture is present within him, he understands: "The enlightenment factor of rapture is present within me";
when the enlightenment factor of rapture is not present within him, he understands: "The enlightenment factor of rapture is not present within me.
He also understands how the unarisen enlightenment factor of rapture comes to arise, and how the arisen enlightenment factor of rapture [is maintained].
There is the fulfillment of the development of the enlightenment factor of rapture, and he understands that.
Or, when the enlightenment factor of tranquility is present within him, he understands: "The enlightenment factor of tranquility is present within me";
or, when the enlightenment factor of tranquility is not present within him, he understands: "The enlightenment factor of tranquility is not present within me."

He understands it; he understands how there comes to be the arising of the unarisen factor of enlightenment of tranquility, and he understands how there comes to be the fulfillment by development of the arisen factor of enlightenment of tranquility.
Or, when the factor of enlightenment of concentration is present within him, he understands: "The factor of enlightenment of concentration is present within me."
He understands it; or, if the enlightenment factor of concentration is not present within him, he understands: "The enlightenment factor of concentration is not present within me.

He understands how there comes to be the arising of the unarisen enlightenment factor of concentration, and he understands how there comes to be the fulfillment by development of the arisen enlightenment factor of concentration.
When the enlightenment factor of equanimity is present within him, he understands: "The enlightenment factor of equanimity is present within me";
when the enlightenment factor of equanimity is not present within him, he understands: "The enlightenment factor of equanimity is not present within me";
and he also understands how the unarisen enlightenment factor of equanimity comes to arise.
And he understands how there comes to be the fulfillment of the development of the arisen factor of equanimity-enlightenment.

Thus he dwells contemplating phenomena among internal phenomena, or he dwells contemplating phenomena among external phenomena, or he dwells contemplating phenomena among both internal and external phenomena;

or he dwells contemplating the nature of arising in phenomena, or he dwells contemplating the nature of passing away in phenomena, or he dwells contemplating the nature of both arising and passing away in phenomena.

Or else, mindfulness that ‘there are phenomena’ is established in him. To this extent he dwells independent, merely for the sake of knowledge and mindfulness, and does not cling to anything in the world.
In this way, monks, a monk dwells contemplating phenomena as phenomena in regard to the seven factors of enlightenment.
The section on the factors of enlightenment is finished.
4.5. The Section on the Truths in the Contemplation of Phenomena Furthermore, monks, a monk dwells contemplating phenomena in phenomena with regard to the four noble truths.
And how, monks, does a monk dwell contemplating phenomena in phenomena with regard to the four noble truths?
In this case, monks, a bhikkhu understands as it really is: ‘This is suffering’; he understands as it really is:
‘This is the origin of suffering’; he understands as it really is: ‘This is the cessation of suffering’; he understands as it really is: ‘This is the way leading to the cessation of suffering.’

Thus he dwells contemplating phenomena in phenomena internally, or he dwells contemplating phenomena in phenomena externally, or he dwells contemplating phenomena in phenomena both internally and externally;

or he dwells contemplating the nature of arising in phenomena, or he dwells contemplating the nature of passing away in phenomena, or he dwells contemplating the nature of both arising and passing away in phenomena.

Or else, mindfulness that ‘there are phenomena’ is established in him. This is merely for the sake of knowledge and mere mindfulness; he dwells independent and does not cling to anything in the world.
In this way too, monks, a monk dwells contemplating phenomena as phenomena in regard to the four noble truths.
The section on the truths is concluded.
The contemplation of phenomena is finished.
Monks, if anyone should develop these four foundations of mindfulness in this way for seven years, one of two fruits may be expected for them:
either final knowledge in this very life, or, if there is a residue remaining, the state of a non-returner.
"Let alone seven years, bhikkhus.
For whoever, bhikkhus, should develop these four foundations of mindfulness thus for six years … five years …"
four years … three years … two years …
"One year...
Let alone one year, monks.

For whoever, monks, should develop these four foundations of mindfulness in this way for seven months, one of two fruits may be expected for him: either final knowledge in this very life or, if there is a residue remaining, the state of non-returning."
"Full knowledge in this very life, or, if there is a residue of clinging, the state of a non-returner.
Let alone seven months, monks;
for whoever, monks, should develop these four foundations of mindfulness in this way for six months … [and so on]."
For five months … for four months … for three months …
For two months … for one month … for half a month …
"Let alone half a month, monks.
For whoever, monks, should develop these four foundations of mindfulness thus for even seven days, one of two fruits may be expected for him:
either final knowledge in this very life, or, if there is a residue remaining, the state of a non-returner."
“Bhikkhus, this is the one-way path for the purification of beings, for the surmounting of sorrow and lamentation,
for the disappearance of pain and grief, for the attainment of the true way, and for the realization of Nibbāna— namely,
the four foundations of mindfulness.”
"Thus, that which was said was spoken with reference to this.
This is what the Blessed One said.
Elated, those bhikkhus rejoiced in the words of the Blessed One.
The *Satipaṭṭhāna Sutta*, the tenth, is finished.
The first chapter, the *Mūlapariyāya Vagga*, is finished.
Here is its summary verse (*uddāna*):
The heirs of the Dhamma who possess the fundamental restraint,
the chapter on fearfulness, the chapter on desire,
the reduction of defilements, right view, and the foundations of mindfulness.
The peerless, perfectly completed, most excellent chapter.
